"Remit" is a formal verb with several distinct meanings. All of them share a common thread: releasing something — letting it go, sending it away, or passing it on. Once you see that thread, the meanings stop feeling random and start making sense together.

Here are all its major meanings, one by one:
1. To send money as payment

This is the meaning you'll encounter most often — in banking, business, and finance.

When you remit money, you send it to someone to pay a bill, clear a debt, or transfer funds, often over a distance.

"Please remit the full amount within 30 days."
"Migrant workers remit billions of dollars to their home countries every year."
"The company failed to remit the taxes it had collected from customers."

The noun form of this meaning is remittance — the money itself that is sent. When you read about "remittances" in the news, it usually refers to money that migrants send back to their families abroad. That word comes directly from this meaning of "remit."
2. To cancel, reduce, or forgive a punishment, debt, or sin

This meaning is used in legal, governmental, and religious contexts. When an authority remits a fine, sentence, or sin, they are either wiping it out entirely or making it less severe — they are letting the person off the hook, fully or partially.

"The governor remitted the prisoner's sentence from death to life imprisonment." (Reduced it — not cancelled, but made less severe.)
"The court remitted the fine after learning of his financial hardship." (Cancelled it.)
"Whose sins you remit, they are remitted." (From the Bible — if you forgive someone's sins, those sins are considered forgiven.)

This is also where the word remission comes from. When a doctor says a cancer patient is "in remission," they mean the disease has pulled back or become much less active — it has been, in a sense, reduced or let go. And when a fever "remits," it means it has gone down or eased off.
3. To refer or send a matter to another authority

This meaning is mostly used in law and formal administration. When a court or committee remits a case or question, it means they pass it along to another body — another court, a working group, an expert panel — for them to deal with, decide, or investigate.

"The Supreme Court remitted the case to the trial court for reconsideration."
"The board remitted the matter to a subcommittee for further review."

Think of it as handing off responsibility. You're not resolving the issue yourself — you're sending it to whoever is better placed or more appropriate to handle it.
4. To postpone or defer (formal/rare)

Less commonly, remit can mean to put something off to a later time. This usage is old-fashioned and mainly appears in formal or official writing.

"The committee remitted the decision until more information became available."

You won't encounter this meaning often in everyday language, but it's worth knowing so you aren't puzzled when you see it.
5. To become less intense or severe on its own (intransitive)

In this use, nothing is being sent away by a person — rather, something (pain, illness, fever, intensity) remits on its own, meaning it eases off, subsides, or temporarily withdraws.

"Her symptoms remitted after three days of treatment."
"The fever remitted toward morning."
"The storm's intensity remitted by noon."

This is closely related to the medical use of remission (a cancer going into remission = the cancer is subsiding, pulling back).
How all these meanings connect

The word "remit" covers a surprisingly wide territory, but notice the common thread:

  • Sending money = releasing funds to someone else
  • Forgiving a punishment = releasing someone from their penalty
  • Referring a case = releasing a matter to another authority
  • Postponing = releasing a decision to a future time
  • Intensity easing = the condition releasing its grip

In every case, something is being let go or passed on. That's the soul of the word.
How formal is "remit"?

Fairly formal. You'd see it in business letters, legal documents, government notices, medical writing, and journalism — not so much in casual conversation. If you told a friend "I'll remit the money tonight," they'd understand you, but it would sound oddly stiff. You'd normally just say "I'll send you the money." But in a business email or a court judgment, "remit" fits naturally.
A note on "remit" as a noun (so you're not caught off guard)

Since you asked only about the verb, this is just a heads-up: "remit" is also used as a noun, especially in British English, where it means the area of responsibility assigned to someone.

"Pricing decisions fall outside my remit." (= That's not my area to handle.)

This is a completely different meaning from the verb and is unrelated to it. You'll mostly encounter this noun form in professional or governmental contexts in British English.
Summary

MeaningExample in a sentence

To send money → "Please remit payment by the end of the month."
To cancel or forgive → "The court remitted his fine." / "The judge remitted half the sentence."
To refer to another authority → "The case was remitted to the lower court."
To postpone → "The decision was remitted to next quarter." (rare, formal)
To ease off on its own → "The fever remitted by morning." (connects to "remission")

The word you'll most often need to use yourself is the first — sending money. The others you'll mostly read in legal, medical, or formal texts, and now you have the tools to understand them when you do.
